subject: maths

moments.title: Ramanujan in obscurity
moments.body:
Ramanujan grows up in Erode, southern India. His family is poor. He gets hold of G.S. Carr's 'Synopsis of Elementary Results in Pure Mathematics' — a dense outline of 5,000 theorems — and works through it on his own.

He fails his college courses (only mathematics interests him). He works as a clerk at the Madras Port Trust. He fills notebooks with thousands of original results in number theory, modular forms, infinite series — most without proof, often without any apparent derivation.
moments.takeaway: A self-taught genius produces mathematics that no Western tradition could have anticipated, in conditions of relative isolation.

moments.title: Letter to Hardy
moments.who: Ramanujan to G. H. Hardy, Cambridge
moments.body:
Ramanujan writes to several British mathematicians. Most ignore him. G. H. Hardy at Cambridge, with his collaborator J.E. Littlewood, reads a 10-page sample of Ramanujan's results.

Some are known. Some are wrong. Some are clearly true and extraordinary — formulas no European mathematician had ever seen.

Hardy: 'They must be true, because, if they were not true, no one would have had the imagination to invent them.'

quote.text: I have found a friend in you who views my labours sympathetically.
quote.attrib: Ramanujan, in his first letter to Hardy, January 1913

moments.takeaway: An obscure Indian clerk produces formulas so original that a Cambridge professor concludes they must be the work of a genius.

moments.title: Ramanujan at Cambridge
moments.body:
Hardy arranges for Ramanujan to come to Cambridge despite Brahmin religious objections to crossing the sea. From 1914 to 1917, Ramanujan publishes prolifically with Hardy: partition functions, mock theta functions, continued fractions, identities involving pi.

He is elected Fellow of the Royal Society in 1918 and Fellow of Trinity College — among the first Indians in either body.

His health declines in England's climate, diet (he is a strict vegetarian) and wartime austerity. He returns to India in 1919, severely ill.
moments.takeaway: Three years of collaboration in Cambridge produce results that mathematicians still mine today.

moments.title: Ramanujan dies, leaving a lost notebook
moments.body:
Ramanujan dies on 26 April 1920, aged 32. Cause variously given as tuberculosis or hepatic amoebiasis. He leaves his final mathematical notebook with his wife.

The 'lost notebook' is rediscovered in 1976 by George Andrews in a box at Trinity College's Wren Library. It contains hundreds of unproven identities involving mock theta functions — a class of functions whose definition Ramanujan never formalised.

The mock theta functions turn out to be examples of mock modular forms, a concept rigorously defined only in 2002 by Sander Zwegers.
moments.takeaway: Ramanujan's mathematics keeps producing surprises a century after his death. He saw structures that no one else could yet conceive of.

now.title: Ramanujan's legacy
now.body:
Ramanujan's notebooks (over 3,900 results) are still being explored. His partition function formulas are exact (Hardy-Ramanujan-Rademacher). His mock theta functions connect to black hole physics (Zwegers, Ono, Bringmann).

His intuition is the subject of ongoing study: how did he produce identities that took decades to prove? Modern collaborations between number theorists and physicists keep finding deep structures in his work.
now.open_questions: How did Ramanujan 'see' results without proof? Are there still major theorems hiding in his notebooks? Can mock modular forms tell us more about quantum gravity? What can we learn about mathematical creativity from his extreme example?

reflection: Ramanujan attributed many of his discoveries to dreams or visions from his family goddess Namagiri. Hardy, an atheist, struggled with this but didn't doubt the quality of the work. How should we account for cultural and spiritual frames that produce extraordinary work? Does the source of inspiration matter, or only the result?
